abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) is an exceptionally rare inflammatory disorder affecting choroid and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Although recent studies suggest an immune-driven nature, the underlying etiology of APMPPE remains elusive. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive investigation on the peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) profile of an APMPPE patient using single-cell RNA sequencing. Our analysis revealed striking transcriptional alterations in monocytes within the PBMCs, identifying five distinct subpopulations: S100A12, CD16, pro-inflammatory, megakaryocyte-like, and NK-like monocyte subsets. Employing pseudotime inference, we observed a shift in APMPPE monocytes towards differentiation into inflammation-associated pro-inflammatory monocytes and a CD16 monocyte trajectory. Furthermore, we identified IFITM3 as a key player in the immune response driving the pathogenesis of APMPPE. Notably, two disease-relevant subgroups of monocytes, pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocytes, were implicated in APMPPE. CD16 monocytes, in particular, were involved in melanogenesis, suggesting that the abnormal expression of melanin in monocytes might result from autoimmune responses against pigment-enriched RPE cells. This study provided a comprehensive view of immune landscape in APMPPE, shedding light on the previously unrecognized contributions of pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocytes to this autoimmune condition.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) is a very rare primary inflammatory choroidopathy. It predominantly affects young adults of both genders, with an estimated annual incidence of 0.15 per 100,000 individuals [1]. The condition was first described by Gass in 1968, who reported multiple, discrete, cream-colored lesions in the posterior pole of three young women experiencing sudden painless vision loss [2, 3]. Early descriptions suggest that the disease is self-limiting, with spontaneous remissions occurring within 6 weeks [4]. However, subsequent reports have revealed cases of recurrent disease and poorer visual outcomes [5, 6]. Multimodal imaging features of APMPPE indicate that the primary inflammatory involvement lies at the choriocapillaris, with secondary photoreceptor disruption contributing to its distinct clinical phenotype [3, 5, 7–9].

The clinical features and diagnostic criteria of APMPPE have been described in several studies [10], however, the precise underlying pathogenesis remains elusive. Initially, inflammation was thought to be occurring at the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and over two-thirds of the patients have been recommended systemic corticosteroid therapy with or without additional non-steroidal immunosuppression [3]. Over the past decades, accumulating evidence supports the hypothesis of an immune-driven nature. Case series typically emphasize the presence of a viral flu-like prodrome prior to the onset of APMPPE and suggest an autoimmune or autoinflammatory response [2, 4, 11–14]. APMPPE has been associated with preexisting autoimmune diseases, including psoriasis, sarcoidosis, erythema nodosum, eczema, and diabetes mellitus. Additionally, it has been reported that some patients developed these conditions after APMPPE diagnosis [1, 15, 16]. A recent genetic study suggests that individuals with susceptibility genes, such as HLA-B7 and HLA-DR2, are prone to APMPPE disease [17]. Nonetheless, the mechanisms by which triggering factors initiate innate immune responses and subsequent inflammation in the choroid and RPE are still unclear. Similarly, it is unclear why pigment-enriched RPE is the main target and why fundus hypo-autofluorescence is the main phenotype of the disease.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) consist of various cell subsets, including monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), and B cells, which function as essential components of the immune system. These cells play crucial roles in the development of inflammatory diseases, angiogenesis, and tumor growth [18–21]. In recent years, single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) has allowed comprehensive profiling of the immune system in an unprecedented way. In this study, we employed scRNA-seq to investigate the immune pathogenesis of APMPPE by analyzing PBMCs obtained from an APMPPE patient in the acute attack and a healthy control. Our findings provide evidence that the immune response and dysfunction of melanogenesis are involved in APMPPE, which shed light on the crucial role of pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocytes in the immunopathogenesis of APMPPE.

sec.title: Clinical features of the APMPPE case
sec.p: A 22-year-old female patient complained of sudden reduced vision in both eyes following evident flu symptoms 2 weeks ago. Serological examination of C-reactive protein, HBV, HCV, HIV, and syphilis yielded negative for the pathogens. Ophthalmic examinations revealed a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 20/32 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye, with no apparent abnormalities in the anterior chamber and vitreous. Multiple yellow-white placoid lesions near the fovea, as well as macular pigmentation, were observed in the fundus of both eyes. The lesions were concentrated in the posterior pole, with blurred borders and some fused together (Supplementary Fig. 1). In fundus autofluorescence (FAF) images, the lesions exhibited hypo-autofluorescent spots against a background of hyper-autofluorescence (Fig. 1A). Swept source optical coherence tomography (OCT) B-scan revealed destruction of the outer retinal layers, absence of the ellipsoid zone and RPE band in the lesion areas (Fig. 1B, Supplementary Fig. 2A). OCT Angio (OCTA) images showed absence of choroidal capillaries locally (Fig. 1C, Supplementary Fig. 2C). Adaptive optical (AO) fundus imaging demonstrated cones atrophy or accumulation of abnormal cone photoreceptors (Fig. 1D, Supplementary Fig. 2G). FFA showed hypofluorescence in the early phase (Fig. 1E) and hyperfluorescence in the late phase (Fig. 1F) corresponding to the lesions. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) showed hypofluorescence from the early to late phases (Fig. 1G, H). Microperimetry revealed decreased retinal photosensitivity in the affected areas of both eyes (Fig. 1I, Supplementary Fig. 2E). Additionally, multifocal electroretinography (mERG) indicated decreased amplitude in the corresponding regions (Fig. 1J, Supplementary Fig. 2I).

sec.p: Follow-up for one month, the BCVA improved significantly to 20/20 in right eye and 20/16 in left eye. Retinal photosensitivity showed significant improvement. Follow-up for 10 months, the BCVA recovered to 20/16 in both eyes. To facilitate observation, we compiled the patients’ baseline and 10-month data for a side-by-side comparison as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. In the 10-month follow-up study overlaid on baseline results, the yellow-white patches in the bilateral fundus became less prominent, although macular pigmentation remained present. OCT B-scan showed the outer layers of the retina had partially recovered, with continuous ellipsoid and RPE bands (Supplementary Fig. 2B). Choroidal capillaries were restored in OCTA (Supplementary Fig. 2D). Nevertheless, the light reflection of cones was not completely recovered in AO imaging, although the sign of cell accumulation was reduced (Supplementary Fig. 2H). Retinal photosensitivity and mERG amplitude in the corresponding areas were restored (Supplementary Fig. 2F, J).

sec.title: Clustering analysis of major PBMC subtypes and cell population identification
sec.p: To provide a comprehensive atlas of human PBMCs in the APMPPE patient, we conducted single-cell RNA sequencing on PBMCs obtained from an APMPPE patient and healthy control (Fig. 2A) during the acute phase of the disease. After quality control, we captured 13,138 cells from the APMPPE patient and 15,566 cells from the control. We performed unsupervised clustering analysis using Seurat and annotated these clusters using SingleR in combination with canonical marker genes. After removing a few unknown cells, the majority of PBMCs were classified into four cell types: B cells (CD19, MS4A1, CD79A, CD79B), monocytes (CD14, S100A12, CLEC12A), NK cells (FCGR3A, NKG7, KLRB1), and T cells (CD3E, CD3D, CD3G) (Fig. 2B, C, Table 1, and Supplementary Fig. 3B). The cell number in each cell type was counted and represented in Supplementary Fig. 3A.

sec.p: To provide a comprehensive understanding of the alternations in PBMCs in APMPPE disease, we conducted a comparative analysis of cell subsets in PBMCs between the APMPPE patient and a healthy control. Using UMAP plots, we observed distinct distribution patterns of individual clusters between the APMPPE patient (left) and control (right) (Fig. 2D). Notably, the most significant changes were observed in the monocyte subpopulation among all subtypes (Fig. 2D). We quantified the proportion of cells in each sample and found high densities of T cells and monocytes in both samples (Fig. 2E and Supplementary Fig. 3C). However, the percentage of monocytes in the PBMCs of the APMPPE patient was markedly reduced compared with that in the normal control (Fig. 2E and Supplementary Fig. 3C). Moreover, we generated a heatmap to visualize the differences in the expression of the top 25 upregulated and downregulated genes in the single-cell gene expression profiles of 4 cluster-specific cells (B cells, T cells, monocytes and NK cells) of the APMPPE patient and the normal control (Supplementary Fig. 4). We performed Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG)-based pathway classification analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in each cell subtype. Our findings revealed that the upregulated genes in monocytes, B cells, T cells, and NK cells were all significantly enriched in the immune system and infectious diseases, which ranked first in monocytes, second in NK cells, and third in B cells (Supplementary Fig. 4). Based on these results, we suggest that immune system and infectious diseases genes are significantly altered in the PBMCs of APMPPE patient, particularly in monocytes.

sec.title: Monocyte subsets were significantly altered in the APMPPE patient
sec.p: Monocytes have been recognized as key contributors to the progression of autoimmune diseases. A recent study revealed abnormalities in peripheral blood monocytes of patients with Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) disease, an autoimmune disease that affects the eye [22]. Specific subsets of monocytes were found to be associated with the disease. In order to gain insights into the alterations of monocytes and their subgroups in the peripheral blood of APMPPE patients, we focused on extracting monocytes for subgroup analysis. The integrated UMAP projection of scRNA-seq data from monocytes derived from an APMPPE patient and a healthy control was shown in Fig. 3A. Initially, monocytes could be divided into two subsets based on the expression of CD14 and CD16 (Fig. 3B), including classical monocytes (CD14 + CD16 dim) and non-classical monocytes (CD14 dim CD16 +) [23]. However, a small population of cells located at the junction of CD16 + monocytes and CD14+ monocytes could not be clustered unbiasedly into a single subset, it mapped closely to intermediate monocytes. To depict the atlas of blood monocytes more accurately in APMPPE patients, we incorporated the precise marker genes identified by Hu et al. [22]. Hu et al. identified a disease-relevant subgroup of proinflammatory monocytes, which showed a discriminative gene expression signature indicative of inflammation, antiviral activity, and pathologic activation, ultimately converting into a pathologic activation state that implicates active inflammation during VKH disease. We identified five distinct subsets of monocytes and analyzed their gene expression profiles. The dot plot showed the marker genes for each monocyte subpopulation (Fig. 3C and Table 2). As shown in Fig. 3C, NK-like monocytes, CD16 monocytes, S100A12 monocytes, and megakaryocyte-like monocytes can clearly be identified. In pro-inflammatory monocytes, however, both pro-inflammatory and HLA markers were present in the majority. As the marker genes for pro-inflammatory were more specific, including unique expression of IFI6, ISG15, IL1B, and IFI44L, we defined them as pro-inflammatory monocytes. We identified five distinct subsets of monocytes, namely NK-like, CD16, pro-inflammatory, megakaryocyte-like, and S100A12 monocytes. Furthermore, each subset exhibited unique gene expression signatures, indicating specific functions.

sec.p: The UMAP plots illustrated the differences in the distribution of monocyte subpopulations between APMPPE patient (left) and control (right) (Fig. 3D). Quantification of the proportion of monocyte subpopulations in each sample is shown in Fig. 3E. The most distinctive expression changes among all monocyte subsets in APMPPE disease patient was the appearance of transcriptional programs associated with a pro-inflammatory state. As shown in Fig. 3D, E, APMPPE disease caused subtype transfers among monocyte subsets. The percentage of pro-inflammatory monocytes was intensified with the acquisition of APMPPE disease, and the percentages of S100A12 monocytes and NK-like monocytes were diminished. Notably, the percentages of CD16 monocytes exhibited a slight decrease, whereas their patterns in UMPA underwent a significant alternation. These findings suggest that pro-inflammatory monocytes may actively contribute to the pathogenesis of APMPPE disease. Our findings suggest that the pro-inflammatory monocyte cluster is a more general state that occurs in connection with ocular/uveal inflammation.

sec.title: Construction of the developmental trajectory of monocytes under pathologic states on the basis of scRNA-seq
sec.p: To investigate the transcriptional dynamics of monocytes differentiation, we performed RNA velocity analysis using scVelo, which calculated the balance between unspliced and spliced mRNAs to evaluate the transition probability of individual cells [24]. Velocities, represented by arrows, were projected onto the UMAP plot, which merged the scRNA-seq datasets based on the similarity between the extrapolated state of a single cell and the static state of adjacent cells (Fig. 4A). Our analysis revealed a differentiation stream originating from S100A12 monocytes, identified as a root cluster, with a dual commitment toward proinflammatory monocytes and NK-like monocytes (Fig. 4Ai, ii). The highest differentiation rate, indicated by the velocity vector length (Fig. 4Aii, inset), was found along two major differentiation trajectories, CD16 monocytes and megakaryocyte-like monocytes, suggesting that proinflammatory monocytes differentiation from the root cluster was driven along these paths toward the putative regenerative CD16 monocytes and megakaryocyte-like monocytes (Fig. 4Aii). CD16 monocytes and megakaryocyte-like monocytes were identified as the terminal differentiation state (Fig. 4Aiii), demonstrating the most advanced progression along pseudotime from the root cells in S100A12 monocytes. Overall, these results suggest a state transition and the differentiation trajectory originating from S100A12 monocytes towards proinflammatory monocytes and NK-like monocytes at the single-cell resolution.

sec.p: To reveal the dynamic changes in the transcriptome of the developing monocytes under pathologic states, we performed pseudotemporal ordering of the single cells using Monocle2. Consistent with the putative state transition directions by RNA velocity, we selected S100A12 monocytes as the initial point (t0) of pseudotime to reconstruct the developmental trajectory of monocytes (Fig. 4B, C). Two major bifurcations were observed from S100A12 monocytes to CD16 monocytes by trajectory analysis (Fig. 4C). By combining pseudotime analysis (Fig. 4B–E), we could conclude the states and relationships among clusters of monocytes. S100A12 monocytes were found to be the beginning of the trajectory, followed by pro-inflammatory monocytes that were evenly distributed in intermediate range of the trajectory branch 1. Of note, NK-like monocytes appeared at the end of trajectory branch 2, while CD16 and megakaryocyte-like monocytes emerged at the two ends of trajectory branch 1 (Fig. 4B, C). Overall, these data suggest a decrease in branch 2 and an increase in branch 1 in APMPPE patients. Based on the two branch nodes of the trajectory, we divided the developmental trajectory of monocytes into five different states (state 1-5) (Fig. 4D). As shown in Fig. 4E and Supplementary Fig. 5A, the most significant change compared to the control group was the conversion of SA100A12 monocytes from state 1 and state 2 to CD16 and proinflammatory monocytes from state 5.

To gain a deeper understanding of the distinct regulatory modules governing gene expression during the development of monocytes under pathologic states, we employed Monocle2 to cluster genes (Fig. 4F). Hierarchical clustering analysis of significantly regulated genes identified four different gene expression modules, including state 3-4-5, pre-branch (state 2), and state 1 of monocytes development. To elucidate the biological processes involved in monocyte development, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis for four different gene expression modules (Fig. 4G). In module 1, we observed upregulation of genes involved in the inflammatory response (e.g., PRKCZ, PTAFR, S100A9, S100A8, IFI16, NLRP3, and IL1B), oxidation-reduction process (e.g., PGD, SH3BGRL3, and NDUFS5), and positive regulation of inflammatory response (e.g., S100A9, S100A8, IL1B; CCR2, and MGST2) in pre-branch (state 2). The genes enriched in module 2 were highly expressed in state 3-4-5 and involved in positive regulation of CD4-positive and alpha-beta T cell differentiation (e.g., ZBTB7B, TNFSF4, and NCKAP1L), viral process (e.g., EPS15, SHC1, F11R, TPR, and ITSN2), and modulation by virus of host cellular process (e.g., KPNA4, KPNB1, and KPNA2). Similarly, module 3 was mainly comprised of gene sets that were highly enriched in state 3-4-5 and involved in viral infection and immune response-related biological process, including the viral process (e.g., ISG15, TNFRSF14, and C1QA), interferon-gamma-mediated signaling pathway (e.g., GBP1, NMI, STAT1, and SP100), type I interferon signaling pathway (e.g., ISG15, IFI6, MYD88, and IFITM3), defense response to virus (e.g., IFITM3, ISG15, IFI44L, and CXCL10), and immune system process (e.g., ISG15, IFITM3, IFI6, and HLA-DRA). Module 4, containing genes that were upregulated in state 1, was involved in positive regulation of viral transcription (e.g., RPL22, RPS8, and RPL5), adaptive immune response (e.g., ZNF683, RNF19B, and CD160), T cell activation (e.g., CD2, CD8A, and ZAP70), and immunoglobulin production (e.g., IGKV1-8, IGKV1-9, and IL7R). Overall, the common and distinct gene regulation patterns were constructed in monocyte development, which contributed to an in-depth understanding of monocyte development processes and the underlying regulatory basis.

Our analysis revealed a differentiation stream originating from S100A12 monocytes, which was identified as a root cluster, with a dual commitment toward CD16 monocytes and NK-like monocytes. Furthermore, there has been evidence that subtype transfers occurred among the monocyte subsets during APMPPE disease, and the conversion of S100A12 monocytes towards pro-inflammatory monocytes and CD16 monocytes may be associated with APMPPE disease.

sec.title: GSVA analysis revealed the significance of melanogenesis in CD16 monocytes in APMPPE pathogenesis
sec.p: To investigate the potential functions of monocyte clusters, we utilized the gene set variation analysis (GSVA) package to export the KEGG pathways from the molecular signature database and perform pathway enrichment analyses. The GSVA data revealed distinct enrichments of signaling pathways among monocyte subsets, indicating that each subset plays a specific function (Fig. 5A). Pro-inflammatory monocytes exhibited heightened expression of several immunology pathways, such as natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity, type I diabetes mellitus, and viral infectious disease Epstein-Barr virus infection. CD16 monocytes displayed significant enrichments in melanogenesis, human papillomavirus infection, Wnt signaling pathway, Rap1 signaling pathway, and Ras signaling pathway (Fig. 5A). Additionally, S100A12 monocytes were enriched in biosynthesis or metabolisms-related signaling pathways, such as alcoholism, steroid-hormone-biosynthesis, ascorbate-and-aldarate-metabolism, etc.

sec.p: Compared with the normal control, the APMPPE patient exhibited an increased expression of various immunologic pathways and a significant inhibition of the melanogenesis pathway in monocytes (Fig. 5B). As shown in Fig. 5C, compared to other monocyte subsets, all of these genes were specially highly expressed in CD16 monocytes, suggesting a critical and distinct role of the melanogenesis pathway associated with CD16 in the pathogenesis of APMPPE.

The human eye is made up of multiple layers of pigmented tissues that are composed primarily of melanin [25]. Studies have shown that the melanocortin system within ocular tissues has a wide range of biological functions, such as controlling immune responses and inflammation, facilitating retinal homeostasis via maintaining blood-retinal barriers, providing neuroprotection in the retina, and controlling abnormal new vessel growth in the choroid and retina. In contrast to its well-established role in the melanogenesis of the skin, the role of melanocortin signaling in uveal melanocyte melanogenesis is unclear [26]. In human skin melanogenesis, UV irradiation is established to induce the expression and secretion of α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH) by keratinocytes adjacent to melanocytes in the epidermal layer. Melanin is synthesized in melanocytes and transported to keratinocytes through a complex process involving several genes and signaling pathways, including PKC, cAMP, MAPK/ERK Kinase (MEK), and Wnt signaling pathways [27, 28]. Considering that UV irradiation does not reach the human choroid, it is not considered to be involved in stimulating α-MSH secretion inside the posterior eye. What happens to α-MSH/MC1R signalling and melanin synthesis in uveal melanocytes remains unclear given that minimal UV light reaches the posterior eye (choroid). For both skin and choroidal melanocytes, secreted α-MSH binds to MC1R and signals through cAMP and phosphorylation of the cAMP response element binding protein (CREB) to increase the expression of microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF). MITF activates the downstream expression of melanogenesis enzymes including tyrosinase (TYR), tyrosinase-related protein 1 (TYRP1), and tyrosinase-related protein 2 (TYRP2), that induce melanin formation within melanosomes [26].

In the melanogenesis pathway, CTNNB1, GNAI3, and Calmodulin (CaM) proteins (CALM2, CALM3, CALML4) were found to be upregulated in monocytes of APMPPE patient, while GNAI2, PRKCB, PLCB2, PRKACA, and CREBBP were downregulated (p < 0.05) (Fig. 5C, D). CREBBP is a nuclear protein that binds to cAMP-response element binding protein (CREB). The surrounding keratinocytes secrete α-MSH, which stimulates the melanocyte MC1R and activates PKA (via cAMP), leading to the upregulation of SOX9 and CREB. These transcription factors work together to regulate the promoter of MITF, which in turn regulates the TYRP2 promoter. Additionally, MITF acts on the TYR promoter to upregulate melanogenesis in melanosomes [29]. During melanogenesis, tyrosinase (TYR) expression is upregulated, and its activity is stimulated by α-MSH through the cAMP pathway. α-MSH/MC1R (and other MCRs) can promote the survival of retinal photoreceptors and RPE and contribute to maintaining the outer and inner blood-retinal barrier (BRB) and retinal homeostasis [26]. Based on the above information, we hypothesize that downregulated proteins, including GNAI2, PRKCB, PLCB2, PRKACA, and CREBBP, may result in the downregulation of MITF, TYR or the cAMP pathway, ultimately leading to the inhibiting melanogenesis in CD16 monocytes. The observed altered regulation of the aforementioned genes in CD16 monocytes suggests that the majority of pathways involved in melanogenesis in CD16 monocytes are implicated in the pathogenesis of APMPPE.

Furthermore, considering the high abundance of melanocytes in both choroid and RPE cells, we hypothesized that infection with a viral flu-like pathogen may trigger an innate immune response that could potentially affect melanogenesis, ultimately resulting in inflammatory responses within the choroid and RPE in APMPPE patient. These findings shed light on the potential mechanisms underlying the development of APMPPE and may have implications for the development of targeted therapies.

sec.title: GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of DEGs in pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocytes
sec.p: To investigate the function of each subtype in monocytes, we further analyzed the DEGs in each subtype. The volcano plots of DEGs among monocyte subsets are presented in Fig. 5E. Apparently, in most of the monocyte subtypes IFI6, LY6E, and IFITM3 were upregulated, and while EEF1A1 and FOLR3 were downregulated in APMPPE patient. As indicated in Fig. 3D, E, the percentage of pro-inflammatory monocytes was intensified with the acquisition of APMPPE disease. To elucidate the underlying functional alternations of pro-inflammatory monocytes in APMPPE patients, we performed GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of the DEGs in the subtype. As shown in Fig. 5F, DEGs in pro-inflammatory monocytes were found to be enriched in various biological processes, including regulation of DC differentiation, immune response, negative regulation of viral genome replication, type-I IFN signaling, response to virus, immune system process, and etc. In addition, KEGG analysis revealed that these DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways associated with infectious diseases caused by viruses (e.g., influenza A, Epstein-Barr virus infection, viral myocarditis and Herpes simplex infection), autoimmune diseases (e.g., allograft rejection, graft-versus-host disease, autoimmune thyroid disease and Type I diabetes mellitus), inflammatory diseases (e.g., Rheumatoid arthritis), and immunology pathways (e.g., antigen processing and presentation, Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation, and intestinal immune network for IgA production) (Supplementary Fig. 5B). These findings suggest that the occurrence of inflammation and immune response in pro-inflammatory monocytes may play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of APMPPE.

Notably, CD16+ monocytes in peripheral blood contribute significantly to the host’s response to viral infections [30]. Based on the GSVA results, we hypothesize that infection with a viral flu-like pathogen may trigger an innate immune response, ultimately resulting in inflammatory responses in APMPPE patient. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the patterns of CD16 monocytes in UMPA undergo significant alternations in APMPPE patient (Fig. 3D). To further verify the crucial role of CD16 monocytes in innate immune response and inflammatory responses, we performed functional enrichment analysis on DEGs in CD16 monocytes. GO enrichment analysis of the DEGs showed that biological processes, including type I IFN signaling, negative regulation of viral genome replication, response to virus, responses to IFN-beta, and defense response to virus, were altered in CD16 monocytes of APMPPE patient (Fig. 5G). Moreover, the enriched pathways in CD16 monocytes were similar to those in pro-inflammatory monocytes, such as infectious diseases caused by viruses, autoimmune diseases, and inflammatory diseases (Supplementary Fig. 5C). Our findings suggest that pro-inflammatory monocytes and CD16 monocytes play a crucial role in promoting inflammation and immune response, which supports the mainstream hypotheses that viral infection may trigger the onset of APMPPE disease.

sec.title: IFITM3 is involved in immune response in the pathogenesis of APMPPE
sec.p: As indicated by Fig. 2D, the monocyte subpopulation exhibited the most prominent alterations among all subtypes in the APMPPE patient. Notably, IFITM3 was identified as the most significantly differentially expressed gene in monocytes of APMPPE patients compared to healthy controls, and was specifically highly expressed in monocytes among PBMC subpopulations (Fig. 6A). IFITM3, an interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3, has previously been identified as an endosomal protein that blocks viral infection [31–33]. The antiviral membrane protein IFITM3 has been shown to be active against influenza A virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) coronavirus, and other viruses [34]. To investigate the role of IFITM3 in APMPPE disease, we examined its expression in APMPPE patient monocytes at the single-cell transcriptomic level. Our results demonstrated that IFITM3 was significantly upregulated in the proinflammatory and CD16 monocyte subpopulations compared to healthy monocytes (Fig. 6B). Furthermore, scVelo analysis revealed a robust expression of nascent, unspliced IFITM3 mRNA, characterized by positive velocities, along pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocytes, indicating induction of IFITM3 mRNA transcription (Fig. 6C). These findings suggest that activation of IFITM3 may drive the differentiation of S100A12 into the pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocyte subpopulation. Additionally, the most consistently and significantly upregulated genes in APMPPE patient monocytes were interferon-induced gene products (e.g., IFITM3, IFITM2, IFITM1, IFI6, and ISG15) and other genes associated with acute inflammation (e.g., LY6E and TYMP) (Fig. 6D).

sec.title: The transcriptional regulation between CD16 and pro-inflammatory monocytes
sec.p: Complemented by transcriptional regulators, we inferred the regulons of monocytes, especially CD16 and pro-inflammatory monocytes, using SCENIC analysis. The regulon activity scoring (regulon activity score, RAS) across monocyte differentiation stages is shown in Fig. 6E. Results indicated that IRF7, STAT1, and STAT2 were the most active transcription factor in pro-inflammatory monocytes and SPI1 is the most active transcription factor in CD16 monocytes (Fig. 6E). Based on the RSS (regulon specificity score, RSS), IRF7, STAT1, and STAT2 were identified as the most specific regulons associated with pro-inflammatory monocytes (Fig. 6F). IRF7, an essential transcriptional regulator of type I interferon (IFN)-dependent immune responses, plays a crucial role in the innate immune response. It regulates the transcription of type I IFN genes and IFN-stimulated genes (ISG) [35]. STAT proteins, especially STAT1 and STAT2, are critical for eliciting IFN responses against viral infection [36]. As a result of the RSS, IRF7, KLF2, and RXRA were identified as the most specific regulons involved in CD16 monocytes (Fig. 6G). Previous reports found that KLF2 inhibits pro-inflammatory activation of monocytes [37].

sec.title: Comparison of cell population communications between APMPPE patient and healthy control
sec.p: We utilized CellChat to compare cell–cell communication patterns between the APMPPE patient and healthy control. Through manifold learning and quantitative contrasts, CellChat identified differentially over-expressed ligands and receptors for each cell group. Our analysis revealed that the signaling pathways of effector CD4T cells were prevalent than those of other immune cells, both in terms of interaction net number and in interaction strength, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 6A and 6B. The heatmap of the differential number of interactions showed a strong inter-association between effector CD4T cells and CD16 monocytes, as well as pro-inflammatory monocytes (Supplementary Fig. 6A). We also compared the information flow (i.e., the overall communication probability) across the two samples. Intriguingly, 30 out of 34 pathways were highly active, albeit at different levels, in both the APMPPE patient and the healthy control (Supplementary Fig. 6C). These likely represent core signaling pathways necessary for peripheral blood leukocytes function independent of the APMPPE disease. Eleven pathways are active in the APMPPE patient, including important pathways for immune response such as TNF [38], MHC-I [39], IFN-II [40], and CD22 [41].

Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α is a vital mediator of systemic inflammation and immune responses [38]. In comparison to the healthy control, the APMPPE patient exhibits a significantly heightened activation of the TNF signaling pathway. A detailed examination of the TNF signaling pathway (Fig. 6H) revealed that effector CD4T cells and memory CD4T cells acted as source cells (i.e., the sender) exclusively in APMPPE patient but not in the healthy control. The heatmap of the TNF signaling pathway showed a strong inter-association between effector CD4T cells and CD16 monocytes, as well as proinflammatory monocytes in the APMPPE patient (Supplementary Fig. 6D). Furthermore, the inter-associations between cytotoxic CD8T cells and CD16 monocytes, as well as proinflammatory monocytes, were alleviated. The violin plot of the expression distribution of signaling genes involved in the TNF signaling network was shown in Fig. 6I. TNFRSF1B, also known as TNFR2, is a member of the TNF receptor superfamily that promotes tumor immune evasion by stimulating various immune suppressive cell types [42]. The violin plot indicated that TNFR2 was most highly expressed in CD16, followed by proinflammatory monocytes (Fig. 6I).

The IFN-II signaling pathway is a noteworthy pathway that mediates diverse immune responses to non-viral pathogens by binding the IFNγ receptor (IFNGR) complex [43]. Consistent with the TNF signaling pathway, the IFN-II signaling network revealed that effector CD4T cells exhibited the properties of source cells (the sender) only in the APMPPE patient, but not in the healthy control (Fig. 6J). Moreover, the heatmap of the IFN-II signaling pathway demonstrated that the inter-associations between mature NK cells and CD16 monocytes, as well as proinflammatory monocytes, were remarkably active in the APMPPE patient (Supplementary Fig. 6E). Notably, IFNGR2 was highly expressed in monocytes, particularly in pro-inflammatory monocytes, followed by CD16 and S100A12 monocytes (Fig. 6K). CellChat approach enables system-level classification and discovery of signaling communication network changes in response to APMPPE disease.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we constructed a detailed atlas of human PBMCs in the acute phase of APMPPE patient, identified four subsets with unique gene expression patterns, and provided a more precise subdivision of monocytes, including S100A12, CD16, pro-inflammatory, NK-like, and megakaryocyte-like monocytes. We also constructed a differentiation trajectory of monocytes and found that subtype transfers occurred among the monocyte subsets during APMPPE disease. Furthermore, we observed remarkably alternations in the gene expression profiles, activation states, and signaling pathways of monocyte subpopulations in the APMPPE patient compared with the healthy control. We identified IFITM3 as a disease-specific signature that was preferentially enriched in the CD16 subset from the APMPPE patient. Notably, aforementioned studies suggest that viral flu-like illness may be the triggering factor initiating innate immune responses, and the melanogenesis pathway may be affected in the innate immune responses, resulting in an inflammatory response along with dysfunction of melanogenesis choroid and RPE. Overall, this study compiled a reference transcriptomic atlas of human PBMCs in the APMPPE patient and verified the differences in cell subsets, gene expression profiles, and signaling pathways of monocytes between the APMPPE patient and the healthy control, providing a foundation for understanding the etiology of APMPPE disease and potential biomarkers.

Previous studies have established that APMPPE is a rare inflammatory disease, classified within the group of choriocapillaritis diseases [5, 8, 10]. The etiology of this disease remains unknown, but evidence accumulated over several decades supports the hypothesis of an immune-driven nature. Multimodal imaging has suggested that inflammatory choroid hypoperfusion or non-perfusion is the predominant cause of the disease process [3, 5, 8, 10, 44]. Single-cell analysis has revealed several DEGs related to immune regulation in this patient, including IFITM3, IFITM2, ISG15, IFI6, IFI44L, and LY6E. Among them, IFITM3, IFITM2, ISG15, IFI6, IFI44L are canonical IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) that play a significant role in defense against viral infection [45]. Previous studies have shown that expression of representative ISGs (IFITM2, IFITM3, IFI6, LY6E, IFI27, and ISG15) in patient PBMCs exhibits strong localization to monocytes [46]. Consistent with previous research, our studies indicate that upregulated genes in monocytes exhibit the greatest enrichment in pathways related to infectious diseases and immune responses. Moreover, monocyte-derived cells have been reported to exert a detrimental role in models of inflammatory disorders, particularly by fueling the inflammation and inducing tissue damage [47]. Therefore, we focused only on the immune responses and inflammatory changes in the transcriptome profile of monocytes. However, since AMPPE is very rare, further studies including more cases are expected to investigate the alteration in the other three subpopulations during APMPPE, including NK, T, and B cells.

Human peripheral blood cells are largely composed of monocytes, which play an important role in inflammatory responses, antigen presentation, immune surveillance, and phagocytosis to prevent pathogen invasion [48, 49]. However, the functional heterogeneity among subsets remains unclear. Herein, we provided a more precise subdivision of monocytes and defined their phenotypes and potential functions by scRNA-seq. Based on markers identified by Hu et al., we identified five clusters in monocytes [22]: CD16 monocytes, NK-like monocytes, S100A12 monocytes, pro-inflammatory monocytes, and megakaryocyte-like monocytes. Notably, we did not identify HLA monocytes, which disagrees with previous findings of monocyte subpopulations [22]. The pro-inflammatory subset displayed the highest levels of HLA-related genes, including unique expression of HLA-DMB and HLA-DMA, suggesting the strongest ability to process and present antigen among CD14-high monocytes [50, 51]. Furthermore, pro-inflammatory monocytes exhibited a unique combination of genes, including chemokine ligands, interleukins, and interferon-induced gene (e.g., CCL3L1, IL1B, IFI6, and ISG15) associated with virus infection, the inflammatory process, and immune response [46, 52, 53]. Given the more specific expression of pro-inflammatory marker genes, we defined this subset as a pro-inflammatory monocyte.

Our study has revealed an increased in pro-inflammatory monocytes in APMPPE patient, along with enhanced immune responses and overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines. These pro-inflammatory monocytes showed a discriminative gene expression signature indicative of inflammation, antiviral activity, and pathologic activation, and converted into a pathologic activation state implicating the active inflammation during VKH disease [22]. Consistently, trajectory inference revealed that subtype transfers occurred among monocyte subsets during APMPPE disease. Specifically, APMPPE monocytes preferentially differentiated into S100A12 monocytes, with a dual commitment toward CD16 monocytes and NK-like monocytes. Notably, CD16 and pro-inflammatory monocytes play a central role in immune response and inflammatory response [22, 54]. The conversion of S100A12 monocytes towards proinflammatory and CD16 monocytes in the APMPPE patient may be associated with the development of the disease.

Human monocytes are crucial components of the innate immune system, responding to environmental stimuli, presenting antigens, and initiating immune responses in various autoimmune diseases, such as Behçet’s disease (BD), Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) disease, and inflammatory bowel disease [55, 56]. APMPPE is often preceded by a viral prodrome, and numerous cases of APMPPE have been reported in patients with a positive tuberculosis immunological test, suggesting an indirect mechanism eliciting an intraocular immune response [2, 4, 11–14]. However, direct investigations of pathogenesis are limited due to the difficulty of obtaining inflamed intraocular tissue. Therefore, circulating immune cells have provided the majority of our understanding of immune processes in human APMPPE. Our study has revealed a previously unexplored landscape of monocytes in human APMPPE patient compared to the healthy control. Two subsets, CD16 and proinflammatory monocytes, captured our attention due to their distinguished changes in gene expression and the subpopulation molecular signature in APMPPE disease. Our analysis of GSVA and KEGG pathways revealed that the DEGs in CD16 and pro-inflammatory monocytes were primarily linked to immunology pathways, infectious diseases caused by viruses, autoimmune diseases, and inflammatory diseases. Notably, proinflammatory monocytes exhibited high expression of IFI44L, ISG15, IFI6, and MX1, genes implicated in immune response, type-I IFN signaling, and response to virus, providing evidence to support the previous hypotheses that viral infection may provoke APMPPE disease through a mechanism of molecular mimicry.

Furthermore, our GSVA analyses showed that the melanogenesis pathway was significantly inhibited in APMPPE compared to healthy control, with melanogenesis-related genes expressed highly in CD16 monocytes compared to other monocyte subsets. As we observed earlier, CTNNB1, GNAI3, and Calmodulin (CaM) proteins (CALM2, CALM3, CALML4) were found to be upregulated in monocytes of APMPPE patient, while GNAI2, PRKCB, PLCB2, PRKACA, and CREBBP were downregulated in the melanogenesis pathway. GNAI2 (G protein subunit alpha i2), a signaling modulator or transducer involved in several transmembrane signaling pathways, plays a vital role in the melanogenesis signaling pathway. Previous studies have suggested that GNAI2 regulates melanocyte development by promoting proliferation and inhibiting apoptosis [57]. PRKCB, a member of the PKC family, encodes PKCβ, which plays a crucial role in both normal melanocyte biology and melanoma pathology [58]. PRKACA encodes a protein-kinase cAMP-activated catalytic subunit A. Notably, the expression of CTNNB1, GNAI3, and Calmodulin (CaM) proteins (CALM1, CALM2, CALM3) was upregulated in monocytes. It has been reported that cPKCs (PKCα, PKCβ, PKCγ) could be activated by calcium and diacylglycerol [59], and we, therefore, speculate that CaM, the calcium-binding messenger proteins, may compete with cPKCs for calcium, leading to a reduction in melanogenesis. CTNNB1 is a multifunctional protein that serves as a transcriptional co-activator in conjunction with canonical Wnt signaling. When the canonical Wnt signaling cascade is inactive, CTNNB1 expression could be inhibited by the destruction complex in the cytoplasm [60]. As a result of the altered regulation of the aforementioned genes in CD16 monocytes, it implies that the majority of pathways involved in melanogenesis in CD16 monocytes play a role in APMPPE pathogenesis.

Previous studies have suggested that immune response mediated by T helper (Th)1 and Th17 cells against tyrosinase family proteins may contribute to the depigmentation of the limbus, choroid, and skin in chronic recurrent VKH disease [61, 62]. A similar mechanism may also explain peripheral iris depigmentation in VKH [63]. Tobaigy et al. reported that adequate control of uveitis associated with chronic recurrent VKH disease with appropriate immunomodulatory agents and perhaps adjuvant rituximab can reverse bilateral peripheral iris depigmentation and improve outcomes [64]. Given the high number of melanocytes in the choroid and REP cells, we hypothesize that viral flu-like illnesses could elicit innate immune responses, and the melanogenesis pathway may be involved in this process, resulting inflammatory reactions to choroid and RPE.

The tight association between IFITM3 and immunity is critical in the context of viral infections, particularly in response to IFN stimulation [65]. During tumor immune/inflammatory responses, IFITM3 expression levels are likely to increase as a secondary effect of IFN. By preventing fusion and blocking viral entry into the cytoplasm, IFITM3 plays a significant role in the progression of viral infections [66, 67]. The binding of viral pathogen-associated molecular patterns to specific host pattern-recognition receptors triggers signaling cascades that induce the expression of virus-responsive genes and pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IFNs, which restrict virus replication and modulate adaptive immunity [32]. Herein, our findings demonstrate a significant upregulation of IFITM3 expression in the proinflammatory and CD16 monocyte subpopulations of the APMPPE patient compared to healthy monocytes. Moreover, ScVelo analysis revealed that IFITM3 activation may trigger S100A12 differentiation into proinflammatory and CD16 monocytes. Previously, Lee et al. reported that IFITM3 phosphorylation upon B cell antigen encounter results in an amplification loop of PI3K at the surface of B cells rather than antiviral effector functions in endosomes. Notably, IFITM3-dependent amplification of PI3K signaling downstream of the BCR is critical for the rapid expansion of B cells with high affinity to antigen [34]. It seems reasonable to speculate that overexpression of IFITM3 may be part of an anti-tumor immune/inflammatory response. The factors such as TNF-α and IFNs not only upregulate IFITM3 expression but also contribute to upregulation of immunosuppressive molecules on both immune and cancer cells in the microenvironment, thus facilitating immune escape [68]. Additionally, Mo et al. have reported that IFNG, a type II interferon, can induce melanogenesis via post-translational regulation of tyrosinase in both mouse and human melanocytic cells. Inhibition of IFNG pathway by the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib or knocking out Stat1 gene abrogated the IFNG-induced melanogenesis [69]. Of note, CellChat approach revealed that the IFN-II signaling network identified effector CD4T cells as source cells (the sender) only in the APMPPE patient, but not in the healthy control. Given that IFNG markedly increasing TYR protein expression, we hypothesized that immune response mediated by CD16 monocytes against tyrosinase family proteins may contribute to the development of APMPPE disease. Furthermore, IFITM3, acting as a PIP3 scaffold in the amplification of PI3K signaling, may be involved in the immune responses to melanocyte attack in the choroid and REP cells.

Our study has several limitations. Firstly, the rarity of APMPPE cases and the lack of accessible ocular tissue specimens confined our analysis to peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples from a single patient. This limited sample size may introduce statistical bias, particularly given the low prevalence of APMPPE. An expanded sample size or access to pathological tissue would likely yield a more accurate representation of the disease process and its underlying molecular mechanisms. We emphasize that the rarity of APMPPE and the challenges of patient recruitment are critical considerations in interpreting our findings. To enhance the robustness of our results, we included a comparative analysis of the clinical phenotype and associated molecular characteristics of APMPPE, specifically highlighting immune responses and inflammatory changes. Comprehensive ophthalmological assessments revealed squamous lesions in the patient’s fundus with irregular margins and indistinct borders. OCT B-scan analysis showed significant disruption of the outer retinal layers, with the ellipsoid zone and RPE band absent in the affected areas. Additionally, OCTA images indicated localized loss of choroidal capillaries. APMPPE is often preceded by a viral prodrome, and numerous cases have been reported in patients with positive tuberculosis immunological tests, suggesting an indirect mechanism that triggers an intraocular immune response [11–14]. In this study, we constructed a comprehensive atlas of PBMCs from patients in the acute phase of the disease using scRNA-seq. Our findings suggest that viral infections may act as catalysts for the autoimmune response characteristic of APMPPE, potentially through the activation of CD16 monocytes. Furthermore, we hypothesize that innate immune responses may influence melanogenesis, contributing to the observed hypo-autofluorescence in the fundus of affected patients. Finally, our study primarily focused on altered monocyte subsets, particularly pro-inflammatory and CD16 monocytes. Future investigations of other subtypes may further elucidate the immune landscape associated with APMPPE.

In conclusion, our study provides an immune landscape of APMPPE at single-cell resolution, identifies the discriminative markers and transitional dynamics of monocyte subtypes, and pinpoints two disease-relevant subgroup-proinflammatory and CD16 monocytes in APMPPE. We suggest that viral infection may have triggered the autoimmune response underlying APMPPE disease by irritating the CD16 monocytes acting as an initiator. Furthermore, we propose that melanogenesis may be affected during the innate immune responses, which may contribute to the fundus hypo-autofluorescent in the patient.

sec.title: Study subjects
sec.p: An APMPPE patient and an age- and gender-marched healthy individual were enrolled. All participants provided written informed consent for the genetic research studies and molecular testing. Written informed consent was obtained for the analysis and publication of the images. PBMCs were collected from the patient and healthy control during the acute phase of the disease. Henan Eye Hospital’s Ethics Committee approved the study protocols (HNEEC-2023(07)). All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations.

sec.title: Ophthalmic examinations
sec.p: Detailed ophthalmic examinations were performed on the patient, including the BCVA, slit lamp microscope, swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT, VG200D, SVision Imaging, Henan, China), FAF, fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), ICGA, Adaptive optical (AO) fundus imaging (rtx1, Imagine Eyes, Orsay, France) and microperimetry (MP-3, Nidek, Japan) examinations. mERG was recorded following the International Society for Clinical Electrophysiology of Vision (ISCEV) standard. The subjects were followed-up for 10 months.

sec.title: PBMCs isolation
sec.p: Purification of the PBMCs from the blood samples followed the manufacturer’s instructions using Ficoll gradient separation (Ficoll-Paque Plus, GE Healthcare, Sweden). PBMCs were cryopreserved at a density of 1 × 106 cells per tube for analysis.

sec.title: 10× genomics single-cell RNA-seq
sec.p: Single cells from each sample were independently processed into single-cell suspensions and libraries were generated on the 10× Genomics system. Single-cell libraries were generated using a GEMCode single-cell instrument and a Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5ʹ GEM, Library & Gel Bead Kit v3.1, according to the kit manufacturer’s protocol (Shanghai OE Biotech Co., Ltd.). Libraries were subjected to quality tests (Fragment Analyzer 2100, Agilent Technologies) and sequencing (Platform: Illumina NovaSeq 6000; read length: 150 bp, paired-end).

sec.title: Alignment and quantification of the scRNA-seq data
sec.p: The Cell Ranger software pipeline (Version 5.0.0) provided by 10× Genomics was used to demultiplex cellular barcodes, map reads to the genome (GRCh38 for human) using the Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR) aligner, and downsample reads as required to generate normalized aggregate data across samples, producing a matrix of gene counts versus cells. Data analysis was performed using the Seurat R package (version 3.1.1) to process the unique molecular identifier (UMI) count matrix. Cells were further filtered according to the following threshold parameters: the total number of expressed genes, 500–9000; UMI/gene numbers out of the limit of mean value ± 2 folds of standard deviations assuming a Gaussian distribution of each cells’ UMI/gene numbers; and a mitochondrial gene ratio of greater than 10%. After the application of these quality control (QC) criteria, 14,537 single cells for APMPPE (3860 cells filtered out from a total of 18,397 cells) and 15,588 single cells for control (3808 cells filtered out from a total of 19,396 cells) remained and were included in downstream analyses. Data of all samples were combined using the merge function of R and standardised using the NormalizeData function of Seurat. Data were normalized using global-scaling normalization (method: LogNormalize, scale. factor = 10.000).

sec.title: Cell identification and clustering analysis
sec.p: Top variable genes were analyzed according to the previously reported method described by Macosko et al. The most variable genes were identified using FindVariableGenes function in Seurat. Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted to reduce the dimensionality of the data using the RunPCA function in Seurat. Graph-based clustering was performed to cluster cells based on their gene expression profiles using the FindClusters function in Seurat. Cells visualization was achieved using a 2-dimensional Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) algorithm with the RunUMAP function in Seurat. Marker genes for each cluster were identified using the FindAllMarkers function in Seurat. For a given cluster, FindAllMarkers identified positive markers compared with all other cells. Then, we employed the R package SingleR to annotate cell type by using the reference transcriptomic datasets ‘Human Primary Cell Atlas’ [70].

sec.title: Identification of differentially expressed genes
sec.p: DEGs (P value < 0.05, |log2foldchange| > 0.58) were identified by using the FindMarkers function in Seurat. GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were performed using R based on the hypergeometric distribution.

sec.title: Gene set variation analysis (GSVA)
sec.p: The GSEABase (version 1.44.0) package was selected to load the gene set file, which was downloaded and processed from the KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp/) for performing GSVA. The signaling pathway activity score was further estimated and assigned to single cells by the GSVA (Version 1.30.0) package [71]. Differential pathway analysis was performed by the Limma (Version 3.38.3) package.

sec.title: Pesudotemperal trajectory analysis
sec.p: Pseudotime analysis was performed on the monocytes cell populations using Monocle 2R package [72]. Gene ordering was performed by genes that were expressed in at least 10 cells, differentially expressed across clusters, and dispersed with a q-value < 0.01. The architecture of the pseudotime trajectory was plotted using the DDRTree dimensionality reduction algorithm.

sec.title: Identification of TFs using SCENIC
sec.p: To identify active TFs in different cell types of monocytes, we carried out a single-cell transcription factor network inference analysis using pySCENIC (Version 0.10.3) as described [73].

sec.title: Cell–cell communication analysis
sec.p: We used CellChatDB (version 1.1.0, https://github.com/sqjin/CellChat) [74] to systematically predict cell–cell communications based on ligand–receptor analysis with default parameters. Receptors or ligands expressed in at least 10% of cells of a given cell type and with a P value < 0.05 were subsequently analyzed. For selected significant receptor–ligand pairs, we applied ggalluvial and circlize R package to visualize interaction links.

sec.p: The raw sequence data reported in this paper have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive (Genomics, Proteomics & Bioinformatics 2021) in National Genomics Data Center (Nucleic Acids Res 2021), China National Center for Bioinformation/Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (GSA: HRA008822) that are publicly accessible at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa. All study data are included in the article and Supplementary files. Code availability: The code can be sent upon request.
